newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan denies rebel capture of southern positions.
newsitem.headline: Sudan denies rebel capture of southern positions.

text.p: Sudan denied in remarks published on Saturday that rebels have gained control of contested areas in the south of the country.

The Sudan al-Hadith newspaper quoted First Vice President Al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh as saying rebel claims that they have captured southern positions were "mere allegations" and that Khartoum's army was in "full control."
There were no details on the towns or positions he was referring to.

Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) chief John Garang said on Thursday in the southern Sudanese town of Yei that its capture by rebels from Sudan's troops was a sign that the rebels would be able to take the main regional town of Juba soon.
Yei is 1,370 km (849 miles) from Khartoum and on the main road to Juba -- the biggest prize in the war between the mainly Christian and animist south and the Moslem, Arabised north.

On Saturday the Sudan news agency SUNA quoted the Sudanese commissioner for refugees, Mohamed Hussein, as saying a large number of refugees from Uganda and Zaire have poured into Juba, and Saleh said Khartoum was ready to provide food and medicine.
They gave no numbers, but Sudan says it is hosting about a million refugees also from Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Chad.
Sudanese rebels said in Asmara on Saturday that they were 50 km (30 miles) from Juba and certain to capture it.
In Nairobi, an SPLA spokesman said on Wednesday that the rebels had recaptured the town of Chali el-Fil near the Ethiopian border from Sudan's forces, shooting down a helicopter gunship.
Saleh denied one of Khartoum's aircraft had been captured and said a Sudanese warplane crash-landed in Juba after a technical failure.

A Sudan army spokesman said four army officers were killed when the plane crashed on Thursday after "carrying out successful air raids on rebel positions in Yei, Kaya and Killo Arbaeen" in the equatoria region of southern Sudan.
There has been no independent confirmation of the reports.
Sudan has accused Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda of direct military support for the rebels, whose attacks have gained momentum since January. The three countries deny the charge.
